title: Implement topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph using depth-first search, producing the order by reversing the post-order of the DFS.

s1_definition.profdef: DFS-based topological sort runs depth-first search from each unvisited node, pushing a node onto a stack only after all its descendants are fully explored, which is its post-order position. Reversing the stack yields a valid topological order. A three-color scheme detects cycles, which would make a valid order impossible.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of resolving dependency chains by fully finishing everything a task depends on before recording that task as done. You dive down each dependency chain to its deepest point, record tasks as they finish, and when you reverse that finish order you get a sequence where every dependency comes before the task needing it.
s1_definition.oneliner: DFS each node, push it after its descendants finish (post-order), then reverse the post-order to get the topological sort; use three colors to catch cycles.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** DFS-based topological sort runs depth-first search from each unvisited node, pushing a node onto a stack only after all its descendants are fully explored, which is its post-order position. Reversing the stack yields a valid topological order. A three-color scheme detects cycles, which would make a valid order impossible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of resolving dependency chains by fully finishing everything a task depends on before recording that task as done. You dive down each dependency chain to its deepest point, record tasks as they finish, and when you reverse that finish order you get a sequence where every dependency comes before the task needing it.

**One line to remember:** DFS each node, push it after its descendants finish (post-order), then reverse the post-order to get the topological sort; use three colors to catch cycles.

sections.s2_technical:
For each unvisited node, run DFS that first recurses into all of the node's successors, then records the node after those recursions return, which is the post-order moment. For example: `for (v : adj.get(u)) dfs(v); stack.push(u);`.

Recording a node only after its descendants guarantees that in the post-order the node appears after everything it points to, so reversing the post-order places every node before its successors, which is the topological order. For example: `while (!stack.isEmpty()) order.add(stack.pop());`.

Cycle detection uses three states: white unvisited, gray in progress on the current path, black finished. Encountering a gray node during recursion means a back edge and thus a cycle, so no valid order exists. For example: `if (state[v] == GRAY) throw cycle;` and set gray on entry, black on exit.

The time is linear in nodes plus edges, and the space is the recursion stack, the explicit output stack, and the state array. A senior nuance is that the reversal is essential because DFS finishes descendants first, so the raw post-order is the opposite of topological order, and that the gray state is what distinguishes a true cycle from merely revisiting an already-finished black node via a different path.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a report-generation pipeline has stages that depend on upstream stages, and the stages must be ordered so dependencies run first. The system must produce that order via DFS post-order. This is exactly how DFS-based topological sort works.

Problem 2 — A misconfigured pipeline could contain a dependency cycle, which must be detected. This is exactly why the three-color scheme is used.

The mini-project builds a `ReportPipelineOrderer` using DFS post-order with cycle detection, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input has four stages where zero precedes one and three, and one precedes two.

Step 1: DFS starts at stage zero, marking it gray, and recurses into its first successor one.

Step 2: Stage one is marked gray and recurses into two, which has no successors, is marked black, and pushed onto the stack first.

Step 3: Back at one, all successors are done, so one is marked black and pushed next.

Step 4: Back at zero, its next successor three has no successors, is marked black, and pushed.

Step 5: Finally zero is marked black and pushed last. The post-order stack from top to bottom is zero, three, one, two.

Step 6: Popping the stack reverses it into the order zero, three, one, two or an equivalent valid order where every dependency precedes its dependent, and no gray node was re-encountered so there is no cycle.

```text
2026-10-26T23:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Report Pipeline Ordering (DFS)
2026-10-26T23:00:00Z [INFO] Pipeline order: [0, 3, 1, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  edges: 0→1, 1→2, 0→3

  DFS push AFTER descendants finish (post-order):
    dfs(0): dfs(1): dfs(2) finish→push 2
                     finish 1→push 1
            dfs(3) finish→push 3
            finish 0→push 0
  stack (top→bottom): 0,3,1,2  = reverse post-order = topo order

  colors: WHITE→GRAY(on path)→BLACK(done); GRAY neighbor ⇒ cycle
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The DFS-based topological sort runs depth-first search from each unvisited node and pushes a node onto a stack only after all of its descendants have been fully explored, which is the node's post-order position. Because a node is recorded only after everything it points to, the post-order places each node after its successors, so reversing the post-order gives a valid topological order where every dependency comes before the node needing it.

The subtle but essential step is the reversal: DFS finishes descendants first, so the raw finish order is the opposite of what I want, and reversing it corrects the direction. For cycle detection I use three colors, white for unvisited, gray for nodes on the current recursion path, and black for finished nodes. If DFS reaches a gray node, that is a back edge and therefore a cycle, so no valid order exists. The gray state is what lets me distinguish a genuine cycle from simply reaching an already-finished black node by another path.

What interviewers check is that I know to reverse the post-order and that I use the gray-versus-black distinction rather than a single visited flag. The algorithm is linear in nodes plus edges. For very deep graphs I mention converting the recursion to an explicit stack to avoid overflow, which is the iterative counterpart.

In my project at National Bank of India, a report-generation pipeline had stages depending on upstream stages, and they had to run in dependency order. DFS post-order produced that order by finishing each stage's dependencies before recording it, and the three-color scheme caught any misconfigured dependency cycle, returning an empty order so the pipeline would not attempt an impossible run.
